examples.title: Paired t test
examples.source: Session 20 lecture example (page 10), before and after values from Session 24 page 26
examples.prompt: Eleven people have maximum percent platelet aggregation measured before and after smoking one cigarette. Assume the differences are Normal. Does smoking change platelet aggregation at the two-sided 0.05 level?

steps.say: This is a paired t test because each of the 11 people was measured twice, once before and once after the cigarette.
The null hypothesis is that smoking one cigarette causes no change in mean platelet aggregation, so the true mean difference is zero.
Each person gives one difference, after minus before. Only person 10 went down.
The differences add to 113, so the mean change is about 10.27 percentage points. The squared deviations add to 636.18, which gives an SD of 7.976.
The standard error is the SD shrunk by the square root of 11, because a mean of 11 differences varies less than one difference.
The mean change is about 4.27 standard errors away from zero. The degrees of freedom are one less than the number of people.
Because 4.2716 is larger than 2.228, reject the null hypothesis. It also passes the 0.002 cutoff of 4.144 but not the 0.001 cutoff, so smoking increases platelet aggregation with P below 0.002.
The R lines repeat the hand work. The t of 4.2716 and df of 10 match, the P value of 0.001633 sits inside the bracket, and the interval misses 0, which agrees with the test rejecting.
